text: So, Oscar is gonna make me die? He hasn't made me die in 12 years, and the doctor is saying, "Oh, I don't know if it's the stress, the finances, the drinking." So, what are we doing saying Oscar could make me die? I've had him for 12 years.

text: Miguel, before we end the call, I did want to go over the answers you gave me on the questionnaire about drug use. Is it okay if we go over that right now?

text: Uh, geez. Yeah, I mean, it's the obvious stuff like my stomach feels sick, I get the body aches, uh, cold, hot, chills. Uh, everything hurts. Everything is in extremes. text: Um, well, you know, I like the way it feels. Um, you know what I mean? When I shoot up my anxiety, goes away, my depression goes away. Uh, things that usually make life really difficult, uh, get a lot easier.

text: And what about your use do you not like?

speaker: client
text: Uh, yeah. I mean, I think everybody who uses at least has some concern of overdosing on some level. Right? Uh, so that's something I'm concerned about is accidentally overdosing. I have a hard time hitting veins sometimes, and I gotta dig around a little bit and I would get worried about, you know, hitting something that I shouldn't or, you know, getting infections.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. So on one hand, using heroin feels like an escape from things you don't want to think about. On the other hand, it puts you at risk for an overdose in infections.

speaker: client
text: Yeah, that's right.

speaker: counsellor
text: So weighing what you like and don't like about your use, where do you want to go from here? What do you want to do differently?

speaker: client
text: I don't know.

speaker: counsellor
text: Well, some patients who inject heroin are interested in a medication called Suboxone. It reduces cravings, withdrawal symptoms without making you high. speaker: client

speaker: client

text: Your housemate may be willing to give you Narcan if they see you overdosing.

speaker: client
text: Yeah, that's what I'm thinking.

speaker: counsellor
text: Anything else you want to do about your use?

speaker: client
text: I would really like a little bit of information on, uh, injecting in my arm.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay. I can email you some information on how to inject in a way that reduces the chance of infection and we also have behavioral health specialists in our clinic who can go over how to reduce harm with you. I bet the syringe exchange has similar resources too.

speaker: client
text: Okay.

text: So it sounds like you have two goals right now. You want to tell your housemate about where you keep the Narcan in case you overdose and you want some information on how to inject safely?

speaker: client

speaker: client

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah, yeah.

speaker: client
text: -one step back, but now it's to step forward and three steps back. [laughs]

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: So, um, is there, yeah, like a support somehow? My daughter is very good and she calls me, but you know, she-she lives in Seattle, she lives-

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah.

speaker: client
text: -far away.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah.

speaker: client
text: So- and I don't wanna impose on my neighbors or my friends.

speaker: counsellor
text: So you'd like to have a little bit more support-

speaker: client
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: counsellor
text: -and a little bit more connection maybe that-

speaker: client
text: Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: -that-that, um, that has to happen. Would you like some suggestions about that?

speaker: client
text: Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: Um, so one of the things that- that we also have here, we-we have- we can get some case- what they call case management services and that might be someone who comes in and checks with you at home and helps you figure out some of the things that might need to be done like you were talking about, give you a little refresher on safety at home-

speaker: client
text: Right.

speaker: counsellor
text: -and, uh, and-and also might help you organize and connect up with other services that might be out there or do things, um, like that. I don't know. What it- how does that sound to you?

speaker: client
text: Yeah, that would be good. Do you think I should try to go back to the Tai Chi?

speaker: counsellor
text: Yes. I was going to say the other thing that I would say- that I would consider because the senior center, and I know you were really active in the senior center before-

speaker: client
text: Yes, great place.

speaker: counsellor
text: -and I'm wondering if you feel like there's support there. They have a lot of activities going on at the senior center that- and I- and I don't know what was in the Tai Chi included that might be- not only serve the purpose of the exercise but really help with some of that support.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. I guess I've kind of gone to the extreme. I tend to do that. [chuckles] Yeah. So, keep moving?

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. It sounds so crazy, doesn't it? Like the- it- when it feels like inside, what you're- what I'm hearing from you is that it feels like inside like moving is unsafe.

speaker: client
text: Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: And-and yet, we know we can't make perfect safety, but we know that the more you move and the more active that you stay, the less likely it is that you're going to fall and the more safe you're going to be.

speaker: client
text: Really?

speaker: counsellor
text: Yes.

speaker: client
text: Oh, okay.

speaker: counsellor
text: Can't prevent all of it-

speaker: client
text: Uh-huh.

speaker: counsellor
text: -but we can make it less likely.

speaker: client
text: Okay. Okay. Okay. I-I'm willing to start again, so to speak.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. It's scary.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. Takes a lot. Takes a lot. And you're the only one that'll- that can know what it is you're willing to work through that fear for.

speaker: client
text: Well, I'm willing to work through my fears and difficulties to be in my little house with my little dog and my little garden. I've been there for- since my husband and I got married, and that's where we lived, and I don't want to give it up yet.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. And that's a strong enough motivator for you and gives you enough purpose that you're willing to like kind of push through that fear that even though it's there and that, that sense of-

speaker: client
text: Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: -concern about being safe.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. I-

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah.

speaker: client
text: -I-I am. And I feel like I have some help.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. Yeah. Well, we can definitely talk about it when you come in again like-

speaker: client
text: Okay.

speaker: counsellor
text: -again, and-and-

speaker: client
text: So, am I being a baby?

speaker: counsellor
text: Not at all.

speaker: client
text: Okay.

speaker: counsellor
text: Not being a baby. This is a pretty normal- this is-

speaker: client
text: Really?

speaker: counsellor
text: -very normal. Absolutely. It's an absolutely normal thing to feel that, and especially when you've suffered something that you have and suffered to it, the stroke and the trying to get rehabbed and trying to find a way to get back home and going through the wobblies, this is perfectly normal.

speaker: client
text: Really?

speaker: counsellor
text: Yes. And actually, you-you have really demonstrated to me anyway, a lot of strength and courage because you have continued to persevere and work through this and not everybody does. And you have found a way to get home and you seem really committed to staying home. So you-you've got a lot of strength there that you're working with.

speaker: client
text: Thank you. Thank you.

speaker: counsellor
text: And we can work together to make sure that-- And-and Dr. Fields too, I know, is very interested in that. We can work together to do what we can to keep you there.

speaker: client
text: Well, and she- she's not going to throw me back into the hospital?

speaker: counsellor
text: Not yet.

speaker: client
text: Not yet? [laughs] Okay. Yeah. I was sort of- I-I was sort of hesitant to tell you-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: -about-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: -this, but, um, uh, I'm sort of glad I did. I'm very glad I did.

speaker: counsellor
text: I'm really glad you did too. I really appreciate it because that's the only way that we can work together-

speaker: client
text: Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: - to help you feel safer. And I hope you're going away home today feeling safer.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. So the-the caseworker is gonna be able to come and refresh-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: -me?

speaker: counsellor
text: We'll get you hooked up.

speaker: client
text: And-and that's-- Yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: I mean, that alone, to know that I have communication that I w- that was my biggest fear that something-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: -would happen and I wouldn't have any-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm.

speaker: client
text: -any way to tell anybody.

speaker: counsellor
text: Good. Well, you've got some good plans and we'll go check it out and make sure they happen.

speaker: client
text: Okay.

speaker: counsellor
text: All right. Thanks.

speaker: counsellor
text: Hi, Mr. Stowe.

speaker: client
text: Hey.

speaker: counsellor
text: How are you doing today? I'm Bruce Berger.

speaker: client
text: Pleasure to meet you.

speaker: counsellor
text: I, uh, I'm a case manager with your health plan. I understand that you came in today to talk about your diabetes.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. I'm supposed to learn how to manage it. I just learned that I got diabetes and apparently, it's pretty bad 'cause, uh, she said my blood sugar was sky high, and then she laid all these huge consequences on things that can happen. That just sounds so disastrous and, uh, and then she told me I gotta do all this stuff. And man, I'm just sort of disappointed right now.

speaker: counsellor
text: So you just- you just saw the doctor and, uh, you know, you sound like you just got blindsided, uh, with, uh, not only how, how frightening this seems that you have diabetes and that, uh, she-- you say she told you a whole lot of things that can happen with your eyes and circulation and all those kinds of things.

speaker: client
text: She mentioned my legs having troubles and-

speaker: counsellor
text: And so you're really kind of reeling right now from, uh, all of that. And you sound a little bit pretty, pretty scared actually.

speaker: client
text: Well, that's, yeah. It's not just being scared, you know. I don't want that to happen to me, but then when I, when-when she reels off all these things I gotta do and I'm sort of going oh, oh, you know, I'm not certain I can even get it done. So it's sort of sitting-- well, you know, I'm sitting here thinking that, oh my God, this is- this is what's gonna happen to me.

speaker: counsellor
text: So it sounds like-

speaker: client
text: And it is discouraging, just like discouraging.

speaker: counsellor
text: So it sounds a lot like, uh, on top of the fact that you've got something you're really scared about having consequences in terms of everything that can happen, what worries you also is all the different things that she told you you're going to need to do to get it under control. Can't imagine doing all those things, so you almost feel like all that bad stuff's gonna happen.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. It looks like a massive task that I'm may not be able to handle. And then, yeah, all this horrible stuff happens to me. I mean, it's- it's a bleak-looking situation and a lot worse.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay. And I-- And what I want to do is help you kind of break this up into some-some doable chunks so that we can get your blood sugar down. I, you know, on the one hand, your doctor is right, you know. Your blood sugar is very high and we do wanna get it down so that we don't have those consequences happen. Uh, and-and there are a number of things that you need to do in order to-to get your blood sugar down. Um, you know, on the other hand, we can take this a step at a time, so it's not so overwhelming.

speaker: counsellor
text: And I'd like you to be able to tell me what kinds of things that you can do right now. You know, for example, there- there's basically three things that need to be worked out with diabetes. Taking your medicine as prescribed. And honestly, if I was gonna work on one thing right away, given that everything seems so overwhelming would probably that-that first, because that'll have the biggest impact. How-how does that sound so far?

speaker: client
text: Well, I don't think too much trouble in taking the medicines, especially since I understand my blood sugar is really high. and-

speaker: counsellor
text: So that's easy to do.

speaker: client
text: Yeah, I'm pretty- I'm pretty good at taking drugs.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. 'Cause it looks like you need to just take your medicine, uh, uh, once a day from-from the prescription. So that sounds doable right now.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. I think I could probably do that.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay. The other things that need to be worked on over time certainly would be changing your eating habits, you know, to eat- eat healthier, uh, not necessarily less, but healthier. And the other thing would be getting, um, some more physical activity. And by the way, that doesn't mean going to a gym. That means things like more walking, maybe using stairs instead of an elevator or an escalator, stuff like that. Uh.

speaker: client
text: Well, she also mentioned monitoring my blood sugar and all this. And that just seemed like a lot of mumbo jambo to me.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. And that really is to give you feedback about how those other things are doing so that it keeps you on task.

speaker: client
text: Oh, okay.

speaker: counsellor
text: So it helps you know that when you're taking your medicine, when you're changing your eating habits, that it's really having an impact on your blood sugar 'cause getting your blood sugar down is going to keep you from having all of those other problems. How does all this-- where does this leave you now right now in terms of how you're feeling?

speaker: client
text: Well, I like it that I, you know, that-that we can do it at a step at a time. I mean, that's-- that relieves some pressure.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay.

speaker: client
text: And being able to talk with you and do this as we go along rather than-- I-I wasn't certain I could just, wham, put this huge program in[chuckles] into effect. Uh, but doing a step at a time and I, you know, that-- getting on the medicine, I don't think that's any big problem. That I can do I am pretty sure.

speaker: counsellor
text: It sounds like you're very committed to that.

speaker: client
text: Yeah. I think I could do that. Uh, as long as there's no big-time side effects, but, uh-

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay, hard part's over. So the good news is no cavities.

speaker: client
text: Oh, great.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yes, always happy to hear that. I do have some concerns though because I'm seeing some irritation in your mouth in the palate that's called nicotinic stomatitis and-

speaker: client
text: That sounds bad.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah, it is. It's some damage to the roof of your mouth that happens from tobacco smoking and so I'm wondering if you can tell me a little bit how-- about how tobacco fits in your life right now.

speaker: client
text: Tobacco. Well, I don't smoke cigarettes. I've never smoked cigarettes. I do go out with my friends. Um, you know, we go out to bars and, you know, we'll have a few drinks and smoke some of those little cigarillo-type things. I mean I wouldn't even think of them as cigars and they're certainly not cigarettes. Um, and I mean I'll have one or two of those in an evening with, uh, with my friends but certainly not 20 or 30 of them a day like you would with cigarettes and that's the only thing that could possibly have anything to do with tobacco.

speaker: counsellor
text: So you've made a decision in your life not to smoke cigarettes, that's something you didn't want to do. It sounds like you're kinda concerned about the health effects of cigarettes. But you have been smoking the little cigarillos at least one or two every time you go out.

speaker: client
text: But that's- that's just like a- a social thing. That's something that my friends and I do. We-- We-- It's not habit or something that I have to have and, you know, talking about one or two when we go out for an evening. Not packs of them.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah, so you're not-- You're not like those chain smokers, you're not smoking packs and packs a day.

speaker: client
text: Oh, no. No.

speaker: counsellor
text: The amount you smoke is so miniscule you can't even imagine that it would cause any harm and yet here it is damaging the roof of your mouth.

speaker: client
text: Well, we've-- you have a point there. Mm, now that you mention it, um, I have started having one or two at work, you know, when we have break since I have a couple of friends at work that smoke and so every time we have a break, you know, we all go out to the- the break place outside, um, and so I- now I go with them and I have one of these Swisher Sweets. Um, I like the peach flavor [unintelligible 00:02:32] they're so cute. But that's really only pretty recently.

speaker: counsellor
text: Uh-huh. So smoking has kind of become a big part of your social life now. When you go out, you're smoking, and even during breaks at work, you're smoking.

speaker: client
text: Well, yeah, yeah. You know now that you say it like that it's true. Um, I am smoking on a daily basis.

speaker: counsellor
text: So aside from that social aspect, what are the things you like about it?

speaker: client
text: Well, it's relaxing and it's just nice to be with people, um. Um, and you know, when, you know, I like to go to Las Vegas, and so when we go to Vegas, it's really fun to go to the cigar bars, is kind of sophisticated and fun and so, you know, it's mostly a social thing.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay.

speaker: client
text: I wouldn't say I was a chain smoker.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay. How about the other side? Have you noticed any not-so-good things about the smoking?

speaker: client
text: Well, I was going to ask you about, um, whitening my teeth because I've noticed that they have more stains on them up than a few years ago, and so I imagine that has something to do with the smoking.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. So we're noticing some pretty negative effects in terms of your oral health with the smoking. Are there any other things that you're concerned about?

speaker: client
text: Um. Well, there's the expense, you know. Wi-with the economy and all, um, I- I have to be careful about my money and so, um, there is the extra expense of if I'm buying more of them than I used to. So the-the money aspect is also a concern.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. So there's your oral health, there's the financial aspect, and then e-earlier you brought up some concerns about smoking cigarettes and how that can be harmful for you.

speaker: client
text: Oh, yeah.

speaker: counsellor
text: Were you aware of the fact that smoking these little cigarillos, the Swisher Sweets, can have some of the same negative health effects?

speaker: client
text: Oh, absolutely not. I mean I thought of it more as a- a fun thing to do with my friends, certainly not a smoking habit or anything that would be harmful.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. So it's kind of surprising to you that something you've been doing and you've been doing more and more of it is actually pretty bad for you.

speaker: client
text: Oh, yes. I checked the box on your form when you asked if I use tobacco, I checked "No," because I never thought of myself as a smoker.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. What do you kind of make of that now that you realize that you're actually a tobacco user and that you might actually be causing some pretty se-serious health effects.

speaker: client
text: I'm really concerned, I mean, I don't want to, um, develop cancer, lung cancer, or any of the awful things that happen from smoking, and, you know, really, until this conversation, I never really thought of myself as a smoker at all. So-

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm.

speaker: client
text: -I'm very concerned.

speaker: counsellor
text: Well, the good news is in terms of the nicotinic stomatitis, at the point in which you stop smoking, you can actually reverse all the negative effects that occurred and you might also know that you can stop the progression of any other diseases that had started, just by quitting smoking.

speaker: client
text: Really?

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. Is that something you'd be interested in?

speaker: client
text: Oh, I would. I really would because, like I said, I'm a brand new smoker. I didn't know I was a smoker until I came to see you.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. Well, if you think about it on a scale of 1 to 10 where 1 is really don't think you could do it at all and 10 is really confident that you could quit if you tried, where do you think you fall?

speaker: client
text: Oh, I think I will probably be in seven or eight. I'm-I'm pretty confident that I could stop doing this.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay, what made you choose seven or eight as opposed to a-a five?

speaker: client
text: Because it's not a part of my daily life. I don't have to have, uh, a smoke when I get up in the morning. I don't smoke 20 or 30 of them a day, so it's not that much exposure and I-I feel pretty confident that I could stop.

speaker: counsellor
text: Mm-hmm. So, it sounds like just to kind of summarize, you've noticed some negative effects of the smoking, you have some concerns about health effects that could occur, there's the financial aspect, and yet you feel pretty confident that you could quit if you tried. So, where do you think we should go from here?

speaker: client
text: Um, I'd really like some more information about quitting. I mean, I've heard there's some-some new medications, there are some new things that can be done to help people make quitting more comfortable and I-I really wanna quit.

speaker: counsellor
text: Okay, well, I'd be happy to talk to you more about that and give you some tips and advice and give you some suggestions about where you can get some support with quitting.

speaker: client
text: That'd be wonderful. Thank you.

speaker: counsellor
text: I really appreciate you talking to me about this today.

speaker: client
text: Thank you.

speaker: client
text: Wow. I can't believe he fell asleep after all of that crying, poor guy.

speaker: counsellor
text: Yeah. Well, the good news is he doesn't have pneumonia. It's just an upper re-respiratory tract infection and a cold. So there's some things you can do to make- to help him get better. You can avoid excessive dust. You can keep him hydrated, avoid over-the-counter cold remedies. Keep him away from people who have flu or cold-like symptoms and avoid smoke. And the last one should be easy because you quit smoking during your pregnancy.

speaker: client
text: Well, you're right. I-I did quit smoking when I was pregnant, but actually, um, a couple of weeks ago, I went out, my mom was able to take Jake for the night and my friends they were having a birthday party and we had a couple of glasses of wine and it felt like old times. So before I knew it, I was out having a cigarette with them. And since then I've been having a couple of cigarettes a day, you know, just at the end of the day after I put Jake to bed. But that sounds like it has nothing to do with what you're talking about, right?

speaker: counsellor
text: No, wait a minute. That has everything to do with what we're talking about. I can't believe at the end of this appointment, you're just slipping in the fact that you've resumed smoking again. That's very, very important information for me to know. And I'd like to spend some time talking about it now.

speaker: client
text: Well, I had no idea that it was such a big deal. I-I didn't think it would have anything to do with Jake getting sick or, you know, hurting him.

speaker: counsellor
text: Come on, Hailey. You're here because you thought he had pneumonia. You're telling me that Jake can't breathe, you're concerned about his breathing. And then you just slip in the fact that you're smoking cigarettes and you think there's no relationship? Do I really need to review all the risks of smoking in front of your-your child or exposing him to secondhand smoke not to mention the risks that you're posing to yourself and your own health?

speaker: client
text: Well, you know, I-I was doing perfectly well. It was just when I went out with my friends and, you know, usually, I'm fine with the cravings. It's just when I have a glass of wine at the end of the day. And if I have more than two or three, I just get that craving for a cigarette. And if I have cigarettes in the house, it just happens. You know, I'm doing pretty good.

speaker: counsellor
text: So it sounds like if you have alcohol, then smoking is very difficult to avoid and you know what you need to do. You need to go home and as your-your son's doctor, I need to tell you you need to go home and throw out those cigarettes. You need to quit.

speaker: client
text: Okay. Um, well, yeah, I-I guess I can throw the cigarettes. And tomorrow night when I have my glass of wine, I'll-I'll just try to avoid that craving.

speaker: counsellor
text: And let's talk some more about wine. You keep throwing wine into the conversation. It sounds like it's become a significant part of your daily routine. How much are you drinking?

speaker: client
text: Only a couple of drinks a night. You know, it's pretty rare if I have anything more than that. It's just my way of relaxing at the end of the day. It's been so stressful since Jake came along. It's just how I fall asleep at the end of the night.

speaker: counsellor
text: Well, no one said motherhood was going to be easy, Hailey. So let's talk about these drinks. Are we talking about the-the low-risk drinking guidelines, one to two standard drinks a night or are we talking about a mug of Margarita's?

speaker: client
text: Well.

speaker: counsellor
text: What are you drinking? What's the quantity that you're drinking.

speaker: client
text: I guess about- I have about a half a glass a night and maybe two. Very rarely I'll have more than that. You know, it just helps me kind of relax.

speaker: counsellor
text: There's other ways to relax. There's yoga. There's deep breathing. You need to stop raising the roof and raise your kid. This is not okay. You're not just worrying about Hailey anymore. It's Hailey and Jake. You're a mom now.

speaker: client
text: I didn't know it was such a big deal. I-I never thought that there would be any impacts on Jake because of it.

speaker: counsellor
text: I'm trying not to be hard on you, Hailey, but I've got to tell you as a position, it's a very big deal. Your drinking and your tobacco use are red flags for me and they need to stop immediately. So we've already talked about your plan for smoking. You're going home. You're throwing out your cigarettes. You're putting on the patches. What's the plan for the alcohol?

speaker: client
text: I guess I'll do the same thing. I'll go home and throw out the bottles of wine and stop having a glass at the end of the day.

speaker: counsellor
text: Sounds good. And if you need to relax, go for a walk, join a moms group, read a book. How about you come back in a week when we have Jake's six months checkup and you can let me know how that quit plan is going.

speaker: client
text: Okay, I'll try my best.

speaker: counsellor
text: Thanks.
